results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** Full AC and the smooth torus, or the essential torus and chosen knot tube, of the Statement.

[F1] Smooth two-sided geometric incompressibility is fundamental-group injectivity, and the smooth Loop construction gives a neat disk on a cut side. The three-sphere is simply connected. [[thm-smooth-loop-theorem-and-incompressibility-criterion-in-orientable-three-manifolds]], [[thm-higher-dimensional-spheres-are-simply-connected]]

[F2] Alexander duality separates an oriented closed torus in $S^3$ into two components. Smooth spheres have parametrized ball sides. Smooth disk windows can be standardized with their full parameters, and ball attachment/removal is supported in the specified receiving collar. [[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]], [[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]], [[lem-choice-free-smooth-parametrized-ball-windows-and-disk-absorption]]

[F3] Essential smooth torus circles are primitive and normalize to affine circles by smooth isotopies. Compact-source embedding isotopies extend smoothly with prescribed compact support. The finite inverse-function argument gives injective common-width smooth coordinate neighborhoods. [[lem-choice-free-smooth-torus-curves-and-annulus-strips]], [[lem-choice-free-isotopy-extension-for-a-compact-smooth-source]], [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]]

[F4] A smooth knot bounding a smooth disk is ambient isotopic to the standard unknot under countable choice. A preferred longitude is the unique primitive parallel of degree one on the knot and zero exterior homology. Exterior gluing has the actual connected-collar van Kampen pushout. [[lem-knot-genus-zero-iff-unknot]], [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]], [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]



1.1 A smooth torus is two-sided: its orientation and that of $S^3$ give a nonzero smooth normal field and its short flow gives a product collar. Alexander duality in [F2] gives $\widetilde H_0(S^3\setminus T;\mathbb Z)\cong H^2(T;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$. The open complement is locally path-connected, so it has exactly two components. Each local collar side belongs to a single component, and each component meets such a side: otherwise it would also be closed in connected $S^3$. Connectedness of $T$ makes these side labels consistent. Their closures are therefore compact smooth manifolds with common boundary $T$. The map $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(S^3)$ is not injective, so [F1] gives an actual smooth compressing disk on one side, neat in that cut-side boundary. Its essential boundary on the torus is nonseparating. [F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

1.2 We need actual ambient control of a supplied solid-torus parameter. Let $e:S^1\times D^2\to S^3$ be any smooth embedding and let $c(\theta)=e(\theta,0)$. The paths $e(\theta,r(t)z)$, with $r(t)>0$ decreasing from one to a small $\epsilon$, are embedding isotopies fixing the core. Project the two transverse derivatives $e_{z_i}(\theta,0)$ onto the normal plane of $c$ in $S^3$ and apply Gram--Schmidt to get a smooth periodic normal frame $v_1,v_2$. Change one disk coordinate sign first if necessary. In that frame their normal derivative matrix $A(\theta)$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal. A concrete normal chart is $$\Phi(\theta,z)=\frac{c(\theta)+z_1v_1(\theta)+z_2v_2(\theta)}{\sqrt{1+|z|^2}}.$$ It is an embedding for one common small disk radius: its derivative at the zero section is invertible, finite inverse-function charts give local injectivity, and compact separation of distinct core parameters gives global injectivity. Write the shrunken map in these coordinates as $(a_\epsilon,n_\epsilon)$. The small periodic lift $a_\epsilon-\theta$ exists, and Taylor's formula gives $a_\epsilon-\theta=O(\epsilon)$ and $n_\epsilon/\epsilon-A(\theta)z=O(\epsilon)$ in $C^1$. Interpolate these two remainders linearly to zero. After rescaling the normal coordinate by $\epsilon$, every map is $C^1$ close to the fixed embedding $(\theta,z)\mapsto(\theta,A(\theta)z)$. This is quantitatively an embedding: on finitely many convex coordinate patches, derivative closeness to an invertible linear map gives a common lower bound on differences by integration along segments; pairs outside those patches are separated by compactness. Thus the interpolation is an embedding isotopy fixing the core. Finally interpolate $A$ to a small scalar identity through upper-triangular matrices with positive diagonal. The resulting image is a round normal tube of $c$. Apply [F3] to these actual compact-source isotopies, stationary at joins. They give an ambient isotopy fixing the core. If the initial solid torus is compactly contained in another ambient manifold, all supports can be chosen inside that manifold. No isotopy theorem for arbitrary three-ball diffeomorphisms is used. [F3, given, construct]

2.1 Cut the disk side at a thin neat disk neighborhood and round the supplied quadrants. Its new boundary is the single smooth sphere obtained by compressing $T$. The cut side is connected: every cut component has boundary, and the entire boundary is that one connected sphere. For the first assertion about components, every cut component meets either a disk face or the old boundary; a component meeting neither would already have been an open-and-closed component of the uncut connected side. The other side of $T$ lies outside the cut side. By smooth Schoenflies the compressed sphere has two ball sides. The cut-side interior is open and closed in one sphere-complement component, hence is that whole component, and its closure is its parametrized ball. Restore the disk neighborhood: this attaches one marked one-handle to that ball. This is an actual parametrized solid torus. To retain the parameters, standardize its two disjoint attaching disks in the ball boundary successively using [F2]'s full-window isotopies, the second supported away from the first; the complement is the corresponding smooth annulus. These boundary isotopies extend radially with an identity inner ball. Their collars match the given handle parameter. The result is the usual ball with one standard handle, equivalently the standard solid torus cut at one meridian disk. This proves the solid-torus-side assertion without recognizing an arbitrary manifold from its group. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 Suppose now that $S^3=V_1\cup_TV_2$ with both $V_i$ parametrized solid tori. In the first parameter write the second meridian as $a\mu_1+b\lambda_1$. Boundary surjectivity onto $\pi_1(V_2)$ and van Kampen eliminate its core generator and give $\pi_1(S^3)\cong\mathbb Z/\langle b\rangle$. Hence $b=\pm1$. By [F3] a boundary isotopy carries that meridian to its affine slope. Inside $D^2\times S^1=V_1$, the formula $(r,\theta)\mapsto(r e^{ia\theta},e^{ib\theta})$ is an embedded annulus between this slope and the core; pull it back through the boundary collar isotopy to obtain the annulus with the ORIGINAL meridian rim. Glue its outer rim to the actual meridian disk in $V_2$ and round their neat seam. This is a smooth spanning disk for the core of $V_1$. By [F4] that core has an orientation-preserving smooth ambient unknot isotopy. Carry $V_1$ through it and apply step 1.2 to the transported parameter. For the standard round unknot the normal tube in the displayed $\Phi$ chart has Clifford-torus boundary; the frame rotation does not change its disk image. Thus the whole torus is carried to a standard Clifford torus by an actual ambient isotopy. Any essential circle carried with it has primitive class $(p,q)$ and normalizes there by [F3]. If both coordinates are nonzero, this is the defined coprime torus knot; if one vanishes, the other is $\pm1$ and the circle bounds a standard meridian disk on one side, hence is the unknot by [F4]. Full AC supplies the countable-choice uses. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 Now assume $T\subset\operatorname{Int}E_K$ is essential. Its two sides in $S^3$ have the connected chosen tube $N(K)$ entirely on one side. A compressing disk from step 1.1 cannot be on the other side, for then it is a smooth compressing disk in $E_K$, contradicting essentiality. Therefore step 2.1 makes the side $V$ CONTAINING $N(K)$ a parametrized solid torus. Let $C$ be its smooth core. If $C$ were the unknot, its ambient unknot isotopy followed by the relative tube control of step 1.2 would identify $V$ with a standard unknotted tube. Its other side would be a solid torus, with a meridian disk lying entirely in $E_K$, again a compression of $T$. Thus $C$ is nontrivial. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, construct]

4.1 Choose the parameter $e_0:S^1\times D^2\to V$ orientation-preserving and orient $C$ by its core coordinate. Its meridian is the positive meridian of $C$. Its product longitude is a degree-one parallel, so it is $\lambda_C+k\mu_C$ for one integer $k$, by [F4]. Precompose with the explicit meridian twist $(\theta,z)\mapsto(\theta,e^{-ik\theta}z)$. This fixes the core and meridian and changes the longitude to exactly $\lambda_C$. Put $e$ equal to this corrected parameter, $P=e^{-1}(K)$ and $N(P)=e^{-1}(N(K))$. These are smooth marked pattern data inside the standard solid torus, and $e(P)=K$ literally. Their actual outer gluing to $E_C$ identifies $\mu_V,\lambda_V$ with $\mu_C,\lambda_C$, not merely with an unmarked peripheral basis. [F3, F4, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 If $P$ were isotopic to the core through smooth ambient isotopies of the solid torus, carry its chosen tube through that isotopy. Apply the compactly supported version of step 1.2 to make that tube a small round tube about the standard core, fixing the outer boundary. Its complement is then the explicit torus product between two concentric tubes. Pulling the product back gives a smooth product between the ACTUAL inner and outer pattern tori. Carry it by $e$: $T$ is boundary-parallel to $\partial E_K$, contradicting essentiality. Therefore $P$ is not isotopic to the core. All assertions preserve the given knot and torus through their specified parameters and actual isotopies; neither winding nonvanishing nor any atoroidal hyperbolization has been assumed. [F3, F4, step 1.2, step 4.1, construct] ∎

**Given:** Full AC, the smooth knot and its actual smooth Seifert-fibered exterior $E$.

[F1] The base is a compact surface with boundary and finitely many exceptional points. After removing their disk neighborhoods the ordinary circle bundle has quotient group the free group on a graph spine. Its filled fiber quotient is the free product of the puncture cyclic groups and the original base free group, with multiplicities given by the actual meridian relations. [[lem-seifert-fiber-quotient-is-finite-orbifold-free-product]], Proof1.1–3.1.

[F2] Knot-exterior homology is $H_1(E;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ with positive-meridian generator and preferred longitude zero. The actual meridian filling recovers simply connected $S^3$, and van Kampen kills precisely that meridian. [[thm-knot-exterior-homology-and-longitude]], [[thm-higher-dimensional-spheres-are-simply-connected]], [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]]

[F3] A smooth Seifert piece over a disk with zero or one exceptional point is a parametrized smooth solid torus, retaining its boundary fiber direction. Ordinary bundles over disks and annuli have the explicit smooth transport trivializations. [[lem-orientable-small-base-seifert-pieces-have-explicit-solid-torus-and-interval-bundle-models]], Proof1.1–2.1.

[F4] Smooth compact surfaces with boundary have actual finite disk-and-band presentations. Equal smooth Seifert boundary-fiber slopes can be matched by boundary isotopies and their product collars glued smoothly. [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-surfaces-have-finite-disk-band-presentations]], [[lem-equal-seifert-boundary-slopes-admit-smooth-fiber-matching-and-gluing]]

[F5] Two parametrized smooth solid tori forming $S^3$ have a common torus ambient isotopic to a Clifford torus; its essential circles become actual torus knots or the unknot. Its proof constructs the unknot disk and tube isotopies, without assuming every orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of $S^3$ isotopic to identity. [[lem-smooth-tori-in-s-three-give-marked-unknotted-or-satellite-models]]



1.1 Let $B$ be the base and $n$ its exceptional-point count. There is exactly one boundary component of $B$, because the inverse image of each base boundary circle is one boundary torus, and $E$ has one boundary torus. Set $r=1-\chi(B)$. Remove the exceptional disks. As in [F1], its graph group has free basis $a_1,\ldots,a_r,c_1,\ldots,c_n$, with the $c_i$ encircling the exceptional disks. Let $h$ be the regular fiber and let $\epsilon_j\in\{1,-1\}$ be its orientation transport around $a_j$. Transport around $c_i$ preserves fiber orientation. Choose lifts of these free generators. They give the actual bundle presentation with relations $a_jha_j^{-1}=h^{\epsilon_j}$ and $[c_i,h]=1$, and no additional relation. To verify absence of a hidden extension relation, pull the bundle over the graph to its universal-cover tree and trivialize successively over its edges. A chosen generator lift identifies the two endpoint fibers by the indicated degree; free edge words introduce no two-cell relation. The fiber group injects: the base graph has no second homotopy, or directly its tree pullback is a product. Restoring each exceptional solid torus adds precisely $c_i^{q_i}h^{\beta_i}=1$, with $q_i\ge2$ and $\gcd(q_i,\beta_i)=1$. Indeed its meridian is primitive in the boundary basis (one base circuit, one fiber), and its base coefficient is $q_i$ in the local model. This is a presentation of the actual exterior, not just its fiber quotient. [F1, F3, F4, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 We supply the finite obstruction used next. For any integers $p,q,s\ge2$, the group $\langle X,Y\mid X^p=Y^q=(XY)^s=1\rangle$ is nontrivial. Put $\alpha=e^{\pi i/p}$, $t_q=2\cos(\pi/q)$ and $t_s=2\cos(\pi/s)$. Choose $x,d$ solving $x+d=t_q$ and $\alpha x+\alpha^{-1}d=t_s$; the determinant $\alpha^{-1}-\alpha$ is nonzero. Set $$A=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&0\\0&\alpha^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}x&1\\xd-1&d\end{pmatrix}.$$ Their determinants are one and their traces, and that of $AB$, are respectively $2\cos(\pi/p),t_q,t_s$. Their distinct eigenvalues are $e^{\pm\pi i/p},e^{\pm\pi i/q},e^{\pm\pi i/s}$. Thus $A^p=B^q=(AB)^s=-I$, so their classes in $PSL_2(\mathbb C)$ satisfy the displayed relations. The class of $A$ has exact order $p$ and is nonidentity. This constructs the needed nontrivial quotient directly, without spherical, Euclidean or hyperbolic triangle uniformization. [construct, algebra]

2.1 Orientability of $E$ makes fiber-orientation transport equal the base-orientation sign: in a product chart, preserving total orientation means that the signs on the base plane and fiber line multiply to $+1$. If $B$ were nonorientable, at least one $\epsilon_j$ would be $-1$. Abelianization of step1.1 would then be a direct sum of the free group on the $a_j$ and the finitely generated abelian group $$Q=\langle h,c_1,\ldots,c_n\mid 2h=0,\ q_i c_i+\beta_i h=0\rangle.$$ This last group is torsion, since $2q_ic_i=0$. It is nonzero: if some $q_i$ is even, send that $c_i$ to one in $\mathbb Z/2$ and all other generators to zero; if every $q_i$ is odd, send $h$ to one and $c_i$ to $\beta_i\bmod2$. Either assignment respects every relation and is onto. This contradicts [F2]'s torsion-free $H_1(E)$. Thus $B$ is orientable. All $\epsilon_j$ are now $+1$. The cone/fiber relation matrix has rational rank $n$, so the first homology rank is $r+1$. Fact [F2] makes $r=0$. The finite disk-and-band spine of $B$ is therefore a tree; successively absorbing its leaf disks and their single connecting bands leaves one disk. Thus $B$ is actually a disk, without an unproved surface classification or a rational-homology-to-manifold recognition assertion. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra, contradiction]

3.1 If $n\le1$, [F3] makes $E$ a smooth solid torus. The chosen knot tube is another parametrized solid torus and together they are the ACTUAL $S^3$. The core-unknot construction in [F5], Proof2.2, applies to that tube core, which is $K$: the other meridian has longitude coefficient $\pm1$, its tube annulus joined to the actual other meridian disk is a smooth spanning disk. Hence $K$ is the unknot. It remains to consider $n\ge2$. On the boundary choose a primitive regular fiber $h$ and one transverse base lift $d$. The punctured-disk boundary word in the fiber quotient is $d=(x_1\cdots x_n)^{-1}$. Write the actual meridian as $h^a d^b$, and put $\gamma=|b|=\Delta(\mu_K,h)$. Primitivity of these torus basis elements follows from the circle-bundle boundary coordinates in [F4]. Killing the meridian and then the fiber gives the quotient $$G=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid x_i^{q_i}=1,\ (x_1\cdots x_n)^\gamma=1\rangle,$$ where the last relation is absent if $\gamma=0$. This group must be trivial because meridian filling gives $S^3$. If $\gamma=0$, it is the nontrivial free product of the $C_{q_i}$, a contradiction. Thus $\gamma\ge1$. All these are based boundary words of the actual filling; a sign or conjugation of the boundary word does not change its normal meridian relation. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 If $n\ge3$, send $x_1,x_2,x_3$ to the classes of $A,B,(AB)^{-1}$ in step2.2 with orders $q_1,q_2,q_3$, and send all other $x_i$ to one. Their product is one, so they satisfy the final relation for EVERY $\gamma$. This contradicts the triviality of $G$. Therefore $n=2$. If $\gamma\ge2$, apply step2.2 with orders $q_1,q_2,\gamma$ directly to $G$, again a contradiction. Hence $\gamma=1$. Then $G$ is the cyclic group of order $\gcd(q_1,q_2)$, by eliminating $x_2=x_1^{-1}$; its triviality gives $\gcd(q_1,q_2)=1$. This proves both the number restriction and the exact meridian-fiber intersection needed for geometric filling. [step 3.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra, contradiction]

5.1 Extend the fibration across the ORIGINAL knot tube, not an unmarked replacement filling. In its meridian/longitude coordinates the fiber slope is $a'\mu_K+b'\lambda_K$ with $|b'|=1$ by step2.3. On $D^2_z\times S^1_w$ the smooth circle action $$t\cdot(z,w)=(e^{ia't}z,e^{ib't}w)$$ has precisely that boundary slope and is free, because $b'=\pm1$. Its core, the actual $K$, is a regular fiber. Use [F4]'s identity-starting boundary isotopies and matching product collars to match this tube fibration with the exterior fibration under their ACTUAL gluing. The isotopies are supported in collars disjoint from the core. Their union is a smooth Seifert fibration of the original $S^3$ with base the two glued disks, hence $S^2$, and just the original two exceptional fibers. All meridian markings remain those of the given knot. [F3, F4, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Choose a smooth simple circle in that base sphere through the regular point corresponding to $K$ and separating the two exceptional points. Such a circle can be constructed as the boundary of a small disk about one exceptional point with a narrow arc to that regular point, rounding the two arc ends in base charts. Its inverse image is a smooth torus containing $K$. The two base disks each have one exceptional point, so their inverse images are parametrized smooth solid tori by [F3]. The fiber $K$ is an essential primitive circle on their common torus, since the regular circle bundle over a circle has the smooth product coordinates of [F4]. Apply [F5]: an actual orientation-preserving ambient isotopy carries that torus to a Clifford torus and its fiber to a coprime torus curve. Moreover the intersection of a regular fiber with each side's meridian is its local multiplicity $q_i$: the transverse meridian disk meets the regular orbit $q_i$ times in the fibered solid-torus model, exactly as computed in [F1]. The two side meridians form a unimodular basis, as [F5]'s van Kampen computation shows. Hence the absolute parameters of this primitive torus curve are $q_1,q_2$, up to interchange. They are at least two, so this is the nontrivial torus-knot case. Together with step2.1 this proves every assertion. No hyperbolization, Stallings fibering, general closed Seifert classification, or isotopy classification of arbitrary diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ has entered. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra] ∎
